title: Fuel uncertainty collides with shipping’s newbuilding boom
summary: A new study confirms that conventional fossil fuels will dominate shipping's energy consumption, projected to comprise 70% of the global fleet's energy by 2050 under current carbon pricing scenarios. Only a drastic carbon penalty of $700 per tonne CO2 equivalent, far exceeding current remedial unit penalties, would significantly reduce fossil fuel reliance to just 13%. This stark analysis exposes the industry's slow decarbonization, ensuring continued high carbon intensity and potential FuelEU Maritime fines for vessels failing to transition.
content:
Shipping’s move away from fossil fuels will remain limited unless carbon pricing rises dramatically, according to a new study from the Global Centre for Maritime Decarbonisation and Boston Consulting Group.

The report, Navigating the Maritime Fuel Transition, models 12 fuel pathways and six engine configurations through to 2050 and concludes that the transition will be shaped less by a single winning fuel than by carbon pricing, hydrogen costs, feedstock availability and the engine choices owners make over the next decade.

Under its base scenario, with an IMO Tier-2 remedial unit penalty of $380 per tonne of CO2 equivalent, conventional fuels remain dominant. By 2050, VLSFO and fossil LNG still account for 40% of fleet energy consumption, while VLSFO combined with onboard carbon capture takes another 30%.

The picture changes sharply if the carbon penalty reaches $700 per tonne by 2050. At that level, GCMD and BCG calculate that new fuels become broadly competitive, accounting for around 61% of shipping energy consumption, with fossil fuels reduced to about 13%.

The study also finds that e-methanol and e-ammonia are far closer economically than often assumed. Ammonia benefits from lower production costs, but that advantage is largely cancelled out by more expensive storage, transport, bunkering and safety requirements. By 2050, both are modelled at around $52/GJ.

Hydrogen is the biggest swing factor, accounting for 54% to 60% of the levelised cost of both e-fuels. If renewable hydrogen falls from the base assumption of around $3/kg to $2/kg by 2050, methanol and ammonia could together provide 36% of global fleet energy demand.

For methanol, biogenic CO2 costs are another critical variable. Cheap bio-methanol could act as a bridge, encouraging owners to order methanol-capable tonnage now and easing a later switch to e-methanol.

The study’s central message is that owners should build optionality rather than place everything on one fuel.

That conclusion closely echoes work released by the Society for Gas as a Marine Fuel, which has just completed lifecycle assessments of LNG, ammonia and methanol.

SGMF likewise declined to crown a winner, arguing that the production pathway can matter as much as the molecule itself. Low-carbon ammonia and renewable methanol offer the deepest decarbonisation potential, LNG remains the most mature near-term option, while methanol benefits from easier storage and handling.

The implications for ordering decisions are significant. GCMD and BCG point out that more than half the ships operating in 2050 will come from orders placed before 2035, a warning which lands neatly alongside comments made this week by famous maritime economist Martin Stopford at Capital Link’s London Shipping & Marine Services Forum.

Shipping has generated roughly $3.1trn in cash since 2021, more than during the celebrated 2004-08 supercycle, Stopford told delegates in London. Around a quarter of that windfall has already been directed towards new ships. The timing worries him most: in 2023 Stopford expected the industry’s big fleet investment wave to arrive in the 2030s. Instead, buoyant markets and overflowing balance sheets have effectively brought that boom forward by around eight years.

Taken together, GCMD, SGMF and Stopford are pointing to the same problem from different angles: shipping knows it must decarbonise, but the economics of the winning pathways are still unsettled.
